analysis.one_liner: Requires defense contractors to sell the Pentagon the parts, tools, and manuals needed to fix the equipment it buys.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill with 5 cosponsors that would require defense contractors to give the Pentagon access to repair parts, tools, and manuals has sat untouched in the House Armed Services Committee since its September 2025 introduction, with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar the Defense Department from signing new contracts unless the manufacturer agrees in writing to provide the military with fair access to the parts, tools, and software needed to diagnose, maintain, and repair its equipment — at prices no higher than what authorized repair shops pay. It would also require a Pentagon review to strip contract terms that lock the military out of repairing its own gear, plus a waiver process for existing programs and a government watchdog report on compliance. In plain terms, it is a "right to repair" law for the Defense Department: the military would no longer have to send equipment back to the manufacturer or its approved shops to get it fixed.
analysis.who_benefits: Troops and military maintenance units gain the ability to fix equipment themselves instead of waiting on manufacturer-approved channels, which improves readiness. Taxpayers gain because the Pentagon would pay no more for repair parts and software than authorized repair shops do, and because in-house repairs are typically cheaper than contractor-run ones. Independent repair contractors who could receive those repair materials also gain new business.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Troops, DoD repair crews, and taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: The Pentagon could not sign a new procurement contract unless the contractor agrees in writing to give the Defense Department fair and reasonable access to all repair materials — parts, tools, and information — used to diagnose, maintain, or repair the goods.

Repair materials must be offered at prices, terms, and conditions no worse than what the manufacturer gives its own authorized repair providers; if the manufacturer sells the part to no one, the government sets a fair price.

The bill defines 'tool' broadly to include the software that pairs parts, calibrates functions, and restores full functionality — the digital locks that currently force equipment back to the manufacturer.
The Defense Secretary must review contracts and modify those containing intellectual property constraints that limit the military's ability to maintain and repair the goods it bought.

Waivers for existing programs are not automatic: the agency head must submit a justification backed by an independent technical risk assessment of cost, schedule, and performance impacts to the congressional defense committees.
The Comptroller General (GAO) must report to Congress within a year of enactment on how well the Defense Department is complying, creating an outside check on implementation.

analysis.who_pays: Equipment manufacturers lose the exclusive — and lucrative — control over repairing their products: they must sell repair parts, tools, and diagnostic software to the government at no markup beyond what authorized shops pay, and surrender intellectual property terms that currently force the military back to them for service. Some of that lost service revenue may be recovered through higher equipment prices on future contracts.

drawbacks.text: The waiver is potentially broad: any program that began before enactment can be exempted, and most major weapon systems were underway long before 2025 — so in practice the requirement would bite mainly on future contracts, leaving legacy fleets on the old terms.

The requirement only applies to new contracts the agency 'may not enter into'; it does not automatically reach repairs of equipment already in the field except through the separate contract-modification review, whose outcome depends on the Pentagon's own discretion.

Enforcement is thin: the bill says the agency head may not sign noncompliant contracts and requires a GAO report, but it specifies no penalty for a contractor that stalls or for an agency that waives too freely.

A good-faith objection supporters must weigh: manufacturers argue that repair data and software locks exist for security, safety, and warranty reasons, and forcing disclosure could raise procurement prices if contractors build the lost service revenue into upfront equipment costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real and the downside is modest. The military owns enormous fleets of digital equipment that only the manufacturer can legally fix today, which costs time and money and hurts readiness; letting the Pentagon's own crews and competitive shops do the work, at prices capped at what authorized providers pay, is a straightforward taxpayer gain. The main concessions to critics — waivers for existing programs and price terms pegged to what authorized shops already charge — narrow the bill's reach but also blunt the argument that it would upend pricing or security. The honest weakness is enforcement and scope: most legacy programs can get waivers, and the bill has no teeth beyond contract eligibility. On balance the costs fall on a concentrated set of manufacturers while the benefits spread across the military budget and the force.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Armed Services Committee the day it was introduced and has not moved since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez introduced the Warrior Right to Repair Act of 2025 on September 4, 2025, joined from the start by Rep. Jen Kiggans of Virginia and Rep. Maggie Goodlander, giving it Republican as well as Democratic sponsorship.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Armed Services, which is the mandatory first stop for defense legislation.

Five members total cosponsored the bill, split 3 Democrats and 2 Republicans, but the Armed Services Committee has taken no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — since referral.

Because Congress is still in session, the bill is not yet dead: it could still be taken up, or its repair-access provisions could be folded into the annual defense authorization bill, though the action record shows nothing moving on its own.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Defense equipment manufacturers are better off so far: the bill that would end their exclusive control over repairs and intellectual property has gone nowhere. Troops and taxpayers keep waiting for the savings and readiness gains the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Defense equipment makers keep repair monopolies

for.name: Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited both Democratic and Republican cosponsors.

for.what_they_did: Signed on after introduction, bringing total support to 5 members from both parties.

against.name: House Armed Services Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled since September 2025.

against.name: Defense equipment manufacturers and OEMs
against.role: Original equipment makers holding repair and intellectual property rights over military electronics and systems
against.what_they_did: Equipment makers have broadly opposed right-to-repair requirements that would force them to share parts, tools, and diagnostic software, since service contracts are a major revenue stream; no formal opposition by this bill appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's five cosponsors split 3 Democrats and 2 Republicans, and it was introduced by a Democrat with a Republican lead cosponsor, but no vote has occurred, so no partisan divide is on record.

industries.note: The bill directly targets their business model of locking repairs to authorized channels: they would have to sell the military the same parts, tools, and calibration software they give approved shops, at those shops' prices, and give up intellectual property contract terms that block military maintenance. This is the industry whose interests the bill curtails; its gain is the public's savings and readiness.

industries.industry: Independent repair providers and defense maintenance contractors
industries.note: The bill allows the Pentagon to pass repair materials to authorized contractors, opening repair work to shops beyond the OEM's own network — new business at the OEM's expense.

analysis.trajectory: Most bills referred to the House Armed Services Committee never reach the floor, and this one has sat untouched for months despite bipartisan sponsorship. Its most realistic path is not a standalone vote but having its repair-access language folded into the annual National Defense Authorization Act, which Congress must pass every year; absent that, expect it to expire quietly at the end of the 119th Congress in January 2027.
